taxonomy.subtopic: Molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and host tissues

questions.stem_html:
An 11-year-old boy develops fever, migratory pain and swelling of large joints, a new apical holosystolic murmur, and purposeless movements 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat. Antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers are elevated. Blood cultures are negative.

Which immune process best explains this syndrome?

options.text_html: Persistent bacterial colonization of the valves creates immune-protected vegetations
Circulating streptococcal immune complexes deposit exclusively in glomeruli
Superantigen-mediated polyclonal T-cell activation causes immediate toxic shock
Direct exotoxin injury destroys basal ganglia neurons and valvular endothelium
Antibodies and T cells directed against streptococcal M-protein epitopes cross-react with cardiac and neural tissues

questions.explanation_html: Streptococcal M-protein epitopes resemble host antigens. Cross-reactive humoral and cellular responses produce pancarditis, migratory arthritis, Sydenham chorea, and other Jones manifestations after group A streptococcal pharyngitis. The delay after pharyngitis and sterile multisystem inflammation indicate type II molecular mimicry rather than ongoing infection.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Acute rheumatic fever is sterile and follows eradicated or resolved pharyngeal infection.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis is a different poststreptococcal syndrome and does not explain carditis and chorea.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Superantigen disease occurs during active infection and has a different acute presentation.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The syndrome is immune mediated through cross-reactivity rather than direct toxin-mediated tissue destruction.

questions.educational_objective: Explain acute rheumatic fever as poststreptococcal molecular mimicry involving cross-reactive antibodies and T cells against heart, joint, skin, and neural tissues.
